panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Low-power H&E of a skin-papule biopsy from Case 1 (Blau syndrome) showing a subcutaneous non-caseating granuloma with epithelioid cells, a hallmark Blau lesion; scale bar 1000 µm. B: High-power H&E of the same Blau-syndrome papule biopsy showing a non-caseating granuloma with a multinucleated giant cell (arrow), the classic Blau histopathology; scale bar 200 µm. C: Clinical photograph of the trunk of the 5-month-old Blau-syndrome patient showing the early-onset papular (tan/red micropapular) rash that was biopsied in A/B. D: Clinical photograph of the left plantar foot of the same 5-month-old Blau-syndrome patient showing the spreading early-onset papular rash described in the text.

in_text_mentions: In her past history, at the age of 5 months, she began to have papules on the trunk (Figure 2C), and then in one month, papules also developed in the upper and lower extremities on both sides (Figure 2D). She had fever up to 39.8 °C but had no arthropathy at that time. Biopsy of the papules revealed non-caseating granuloma with multinucleated giant cells (Figure 2A,B) [6]. Blood angiotensin-converting enzyme was elevated to 25.5 IU/L and lysozyme elevated to 14.3 μg/mL. In 3 months, the papules resolved spontaneously to leave mild pigmentation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 7 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G). A: Clinical photograph of patient no. 7 (one of the 11 children in the cohort) showing the classic Blau syndrome triad component of boggy polyarticular synovitis of wrists, elbows and small hand joints with camptodactyly, directly captioned for Blau syndrome. B: Close-up clinical photograph of patient no. 7's hand, grouped with panel A in the caption, showing boggy small-joint swelling and camptodactyly - classic Blau syndrome arthritis in a child from the cohort. C: The mother of patient no. 7 (autosomal-dominant familial Blau syndrome) shows extreme deformities of the small joints of the hands, i.e. chronic camptodactyly/deforming boggy synovitis typical of Blau syndrome; a real patient image directly captioned. D: The elder sister of patient no. 7 (familial Blau syndrome) shows extreme deformities of the small joints of the hands - chronic camptodactyly/deforming arthritis typical of Blau syndrome; a real patient image...

(E) Residual joint deformities of bilateral foot and knee as well as small joints of hands in patient no. 11. (F) Micropapular rash on trunk in patient no. 10. in_text_mentions: dermatitis, and uveitis was present in 6/11 (54.5%) children. All patients had wrist and ankle involvement. The characteristic “boggy” swelling of the joints was noted in nine (81.8%). Tenosynovitis of tendons resulting in contractures, deformities of the small joints, and erosive joints was seen in five (45%) patients (patient nos. 1, 4, 7, 8, and 10)—these patients had had significant delays in diagnosis. Camptodactyly was observed in seven (63.6%) patients. A history of micropapular rash was noted in eight (73%) patients. It was reported to be milder and improved at follow-up ( Figure 1 ).

While musculoskeletal ultrasound study revealed massive effusion and synovial hyperplasia surrounding extensor tendons in the wrists and para-tendon spaces around bilateral ankle joints (Fig. 1C), the “boggy” joints were disproportionally painless. Evidence of joint effusion and synovial hyperplasia was also noted among many of her prox

ted since she was 6-months-old. Emollients and topical steroid were prescribed for the control of her skin lesions with limited effect. Multiple brownish annular infiltrative plaques without pruritus or pain was noted months before her initial visit to our clinic (Fig. 1D and E). No uveitis or intraocular inflammation were recognized during ophthalmic examination. No episodes of prolong fever or fever without source before her visit was recalled by her parents. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Real patient slit-lamp photograph of the right anterior segment. The caption describes high reflective deposits behind the cornea, consistent with keratic precipitates/anterior uveitis, a recognized Blau syndrome ocular manifestation. b: Real patient slit-lamp photograph of the left anterior segment showing KP(+), posterior synechiae, irregular pupil, and lens opacity.
